item.title: Trapdoor Computing
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: Computing with values whose meaning is hidden behind a one-way trapdoor. Cipher maps, Bernoulli types, and encrypted search.
item.content:encoded:
A paradigm for computing with values whose meaning is hidden behind a one-way trapdoor.

A cipher map is a total function on bit strings. Every input produces output. The concepts of “domain,” “correct,” and “incorrect” only exist on the trusted machine that holds the decoder. The untrusted machine sees only opaque bits flowing through opaque lookup tables. It cannot distinguish signal from noise.

Four Properties of a Cipher Map

A cipher map f-hat implementing a latent function f satisfies:

  1. Totality: f-hat is defined on all inputs (bits in, bits out). Out-of-domain inputs produce random output.
  2. Representation Uniformity: Each domain value has multiple encodings, delta-close to uniform, preventing frequency analysis.
  3. Correctness: For in-domain inputs, decode(f-hat(encode(x))) = f(x) with probability at least 1 - eta.
  4. Composability: Composing cipher maps compounds error predictably: eta_total = 1 - (1 - eta_f)(1 - eta_g).

Foundations

The framework builds on four theoretical pillars:

  • The Bernoulli Model: latent/observed duality, confusion matrices, HashSet construction achieving -log_2(epsilon) bits per element
  • Noisy Turing Machines: composing Bernoulli logic gates, interval arithmetic for error propagation through circuits
  • Trapdoor Boolean Algebra: approximate homomorphism from powerset to bit strings via cryptographic hash, marginal uniformity
  • Entropy Maps: prefix-free hash codes for function approximation, mu = H(Y) space bound, two-level hash construction

Papers

The research program spans a CS thesis, IEEE publication, and several preprints developing the algebra of encrypted computation.
